utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Mr. Nicholls will be handling the next witness and will be ready in just a moment. I just wanted to raise one issue and just address the witnesses for this week so the Court is aware of the schedule for this week. We had planned -- this is of course a short week because we're not sitting on Friday. We had planned three witnesses for the week. It has not been concluded yet, but I expect that we will agree on one of the three, the shortest of the three, we will agree that the witness need not be called, and if the Court agrees, that the statement can go in pursuant to 89(F). That leaves us with two witnesses for the week. This agreement is -- as I said, it's not even concluded yet and it came up at a point when it was too late to fill in another witness. I actually expect that these two witnesses will be pretty substantial, pretty lengthy and that we may end up filling the week with these two witnesses. So I just wanted to alert the Court to that schedule. And now I leave it to Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, thank you for that and that is opportune by way of introduction to another matter I must raise. Toward the end of last week we looked forward over the next two or three weeks to the sitting programme. Since then, I am afraid, it has become evident that I cannot sit on Thursday, the 17th of this month. I had indicated I could not sit on Friday. Well, I still cannot sit on Friday, but I cannot sit on Thursday either. The upside for everyone else is that you have an even longer break, taken with the week following. The downside for me is to keep the extra time down to one day, on the Thursday I must sit from 8.30 in the morning to the evening with Judges Orie and Kwon to deal with another important matter. But by that sacrifice, the interference with your endeavours is limited to one day. I'm apologetic to the accused in particular for this further interruption, but as with the delay with starting today, there are other demands on the time of the Court and the members of the Chamber, and this is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just address one point about what the Court has just told us. We will of course endeavour to fill the three days. And I believe that will not be a problem. What we have to try to avoid, of course, is a witness carrying over the break and so we'll do our best. We may finish a bit early on Wednesday, but I think actually that we should be able to fill those three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we look to Mr. Nicholls for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're ready if the witness could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please make the affirmation which is on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Nicholls will ask you some questions to start with. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me, Mr. Karpuzi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If at any time you have trouble hearing me or understanding me, please let me know. Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: My name is Ruzhdi Karpuzi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you spell it for me, please.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: R-u-z-h-d-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you some questions about your background in a moment and about 1998 in a moment, but first I have a couple preliminary questions. Did you receive a subpoena from this Honourable Trial Chamber requiring you to testify here today?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've also given a statement to an ICTY investigator on the 19th and 21st of July, 2003. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you truthful to the best of your belief and memory when you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You and I met yesterday and you read over your statement in your own language. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you made a few corrections to your earlier statement in a statement which you signed yesterday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you also truthful in the statement which you made yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I have always tried to tell the truth, and I am telling here again that I have told the truth as much as I remember, as much as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll ask a few questions about your background. Could you tell me when and where you were born, please.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I was born on January 23rd, 1965, in Shale village commune, Lipjan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which village do you live in today?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I continue to live in Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I have two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber about your educational background, I mean how far you went in school.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, Distinguished Tribunal, I finished the primary school and then two years of the high school, because I couldn't go on with my studies due to Serb repression which deprived us of the right to schooling, finding various pretexts to prevent us. So that's my education.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you perform your compulsory military service in 1988?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: In Zagreb in the former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long did that military service last?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: This military service continued for one year. Then I did three more months further to that military service for no other reason than being Albanian. They found reasons, pretexts, to make us do extra military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while you were in the military in 1988, did you receive any specialised training, any training in any particular specialty?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: The Yugoslav service was such that we were trained in various areas. When I was doing my service, I was in the anti-tank unit Poc was called in Serbian, in short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a couple questions about any political involvement you may have had. In 1990/1991, that time frame, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which party was that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: At the beginning there was no other political party -- at least I didn't know of existence of any other, so I joined the LDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you currently involved in politics in any way?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I am a member of the PDK after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And are you currently involved in your village in any way in the village council?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm deputy chairman of the village council in Shale village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you just briefly tell us what that entails, what your duties are as deputy chairman.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. The village council looks after all the problems facing the inhabitants of the village, that is it takes care of all the problems that the village has, the needs they have. That's it, more or less what they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit now about your employment, past employment. Were you employed from 1988 after you finished your military service? Could you tell us what kind of work you did during that period.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I used to work in 1985 in Golesh magnesium mine. Then I did my military service for 12 plus three months. After I returned from the military service, I went back to the same place I used to work in the past; but at that time we were involved in protests. We staged a sit-on strike in the Golesh mine against the amendments to the constitution. We stayed there for eight days and eight nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what year did that take place in, this strike? Or this protest, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: That was in 1989. I can't give you an accurate date. It must have been 8th or 21st of February. I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell me - you started talking about this earlier - but what life was like for your -- for you and your family after 1988 under the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It was a very hard life. We were treated like secondary-rate citizens without any reasons for that. They might come to your home. They might maltreat you in the very eyes of your family. In some instances this happened also during the -- our employment. When we left work and -- or when we wanted to go to work and get on a bus, without any reasons the police officers might take you away from the bus, beat you, and denounce you for failing to report to work. Life was very hard indeed in that period, but before the Serb forces withdrew from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you ever personally, as you said, maltreated in the very eyes of your family?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I was not once but two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe what that maltreatment was.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: They always found a pretext, as I said, when they wanted to maltreat you before the family. For example, Why did you take place [as interpreted] in the strike or in the demonstration? Why find or found other pretexts, as I said, to beat you in the eyes of the family and very badly, they beat you very badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you ever been in prison?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell me when that happened to you.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: This happened from 1988 to 1993 or 1994 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how many times were you put in prison during that time period that you've just told us, 1988 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Five times I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And for what offence? What did they say you had done?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: For example, Why did you participate in the strike in the mine? First time. Second time, Why did you protest against the amendments to the constitution? The third time, for taking part in the demonstrations when we wanted to show to the world what we were going through under the Serb authorities. For them -- for these reasons I was condemned several times, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask you some questions about your involvement with the KLA. When did you first hear of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I heard of the KLA for the first time when teacher Halit Geci was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately when that happened?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: The date -- I don't remember the date actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you hear about the KLA in connection with that incident?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: At that time the KLA came out in the open, so to say, through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you personally read about the KLA in newspapers or magazines during this time?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I remember when I saw them -- I heard about them on television. To tell you the truth, I didn't have much time to deal with these things. I had my own problems to tend to. Life, as I said, was hard so you didn't think of doing many things other than surviving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. At some point did you make the decision -- did you decide to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: This was after the killing of a legendary commander Adem Jashari. When he laid down his life together with the lives of his family for our freedom, I felt it my moral obligation to render my contribution as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so what did you do to join? How did you go about joining the KLA after you'd made this decision?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: After I made up my mind to join the KLA, I saw the ways how to contact KLA members because in our region there were no KLA members. So I decided to go to lower Drenica -- several times I went, in fact -- and met with some KLA members. And I felt very pleased with myself for making that decision and for seeing that the KLA really existed. Even though we didn't want the fight, even though it was a last remedy to our question, that was, as I said, the last means that we resorted to; I still was happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the village in Drenica that you went to when you tried to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Likovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who did you meet there?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I met some KLA members. To my knowledge, there was someone called Raketa who took down my personal details, and he said that We know all the people want to fight, but we regret that we cannot take you now because we don't have enough weapons, ammunitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said earlier that you went several times in fact to the Drenica. Can you --

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you explain that a little bit about the other times that you returned to Likovc.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Every time I went there I met some members of the KLA. I greeted -- they greeted me very warmly, and they liked it that people were interested to join them. This is how it went. Each time I went there, they regretted that they couldn't give me a weapon and they asked me whether I was in a position to find a weapon myself. Only then they told me I could join them. So it was a voluntary subscription -- joining.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember what date it was that you were able to formally join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, 18th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At that time were you issued with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't give me ammunitions, only a small-calibre hunting gun they gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about a uniform?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you describe, please, immediately after April 18th when you joined, what were your duties? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: During that period I stayed in Likovc my duty was to reconnoitre the terrain, see how many Serb forces were passing through in the direction of Skenderaj, what means they had. These were my duties as a new recruit officer, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you given any training or instruction on how to perform these duties?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Our duty was, as I said, to see how many vehicles were passing by, whether the Serb paramilitary or military forces were approaching the village or were trying to enter the village, or to go to houses we could see from the place we were located to find out whether they were committing some massacres and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. My question -- maybe I wasn't completely clear -- was: Did anybody give you any instructions on how to perform these tasks?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I'm not very clear about the instructions. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just mean: Did anybody tell you where to go, what to look for? Any type of instruction on how you were to perform these duties of protecting the village?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: At the beginning, no. Together with other comrades we were there. One of them who had been there for a longer time, they told me to go with them and showed me where to stay, what to do, not anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you know a man named Sulejman Selimi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was -- does he have a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, his pseudonym was Sultani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you met him in person ever?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: During that period, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you please describe that meeting, what happened at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember accurately the number. I think we were about 20 soldiers. One day he told us, Guys, we are members of the Kosova Liberation Army. Our duty is to protect the people. We have sacrificed our lives to protect the people, therefore your duty is to be very polite with the civilian population, to defend them. We are their sons. These were more or less the words he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was Sultan's position at that time in Likovc?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I remember he was a commander of a firing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During this point in time around April 1998, how common was it for soldiers, KLA soldiers, to use pseudonyms?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It was quite common because -- and the reason for that was because we as members of the KLA should have a pseudonym, because if others knew who we were, the respective families -- not only the respective families but the whole neighbourhood and the village would have been burned to ashes by the Serbian forces. That's why we had the pseudonyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you use a pseudonym in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was your pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: My pseudonym was Shala. I didn't choose this pseudonym; the soldiers who were there referred to me, This guy from Shala, go and ask this guy from Shala. This is how it came that I assumed this pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, This guy from Shala, meaning this guy from the village of Shala where you were from?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now some questions about the next month, May 1998. Right now talking about the first week in May 1998, do you remember where you were?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was on temporary leave to see my family, to inform them that I had joined the KLA. So I remember it was the first week of May for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And temporary leave to see your family. Which village were you in when you were visiting your family?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: In Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now about May 8th. Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened on May 8th, 1998, with you? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: As I said earlier, on the 8th of May I was home to see my family to inform them that I had joined the KLA. Then when I was there I heard detonations and then I felt it an obligation to leave my family and to go and help those people who were fighting. I didn't know who was fighting, I just knew that there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you learn where the fighting was taking place, where the fighting was?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It was in the direction of Komorane, Nekovce. When I went there in person, I saw that the fighting was taking place in Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us please as much as you remember exactly how you got from your village, Shale, to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I went by my own tractor. I drove up to the vicinity of Kizhareke village where I could hear very strong shelling. And then I took up a route through the mountain and then I met some KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the KLA members you met?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, three of them, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us who they were, please.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They were Ymer Alushani, Enver Mulaku, and Ramadan Zogu. There were two others, but their names I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know if Ymer Alushani had a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, his pseudonym was Voglushi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you met these five other KLA soldiers you've just told us about, what did the six of you do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I arrived a little bit late. They were already fighting when I went there. When I joined them they didn't know where I was from, but there were many -- they were looking for someone to help them. They didn't have enough munitions. I started to fight them [as interpreted] even though at that moment I didn't know them. Then afterwards, on the next day and afterwards I started to know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think there might be a mistake in the transcript. It says "I started to fight them." I think it should be I started to fight with them. Is that right that you started to fight alongside --

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I meant I joined them in the fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where were you, as precisely as you can remember, when you began fighting with these men?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain. There is this road Pristina-Peja road. It's on the left side of this road. There is a rock, a very big rock. In the vicinity of that rock there was a place. We didn't -- we couldn't stay in one place alone, we had to move in order to fight the Serbs. We had to change positions from here to here for the Serbs to think we were more in number than we really were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before this date, had you ever been to Lapusnik before?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No, I'd never been there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe the battle, how it was from your perspective that day.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: There is only bad fighting. I don't know. The fighting was very fierce, in fact. We who were positioned on the left side of the road -- there was firing coming on both sides, on the left and on the right side of the road. So this is how fighting went on until the evening. They used all means -- all the means they had at their disposal, heavy artillery, heavy weapons, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you say "on the left side of the road." The left side of the road if you're going in which direction?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: In the direction of Pristina to Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long did this fierce fighting continue for?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Until evening of that day. They went on the next day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long -- how many days in total did the battle last?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: On the 8th and on the 9th. You mean about that fighting in Lapusnik gorge?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, after the 8th and 9th, did you say in Lapusnik or did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I stayed in Lapusnik all the time until I was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll talk about when you were injured later, but what was the date, what was the time, of your injury?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I was injured on the 26th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After May 9th, after the battle ended, did you communicate further with Commander Selimi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you -- let me ask that again. Did Commander Selimi know that you were staying in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: He knew only that I was visiting my family. He did not know that I stopped there. Then I -- through someone who was there, I -- a soldier, I informed him -- because as friends we had to inform each other whether we are leaving the unit, whether we are going home, so that the unit knew the whereabouts of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you receive any response from Commander Selimi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I did not wait for an answer, I just informed him that I am alive and that I had stayed in Lapusnik gorge. This is what I told him through that soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. I just wonder if you received any messages in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. return.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I did not receive any messages from him, but I also knew that he had no grounds to object to it. I had to inform and I informed him that I am alive and that I was in the Lapusnik gorge. So he had no reason to say why I stayed there and why I didn't go back to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you received no message at all. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: There was no need for somebody to send me a message, whether I should stay or not. The important thing was for him to know where I was and he knew where I was. So that was, in itself, an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after the battle, was there any activity undertaken to defend Lapusnik from further attacks?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I'm not clear about your question, about the fighting. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I mean, after the battle ended - let me put it this way - what were you told to do as a soldier after May 9th?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Nobody told me what to do. I stayed in the Lapusnik gorge to protect that population there, and all the people who were there -- some of the Lapusnik villagers invited us to their homes and gave us to eat. And some of them joined the -- our group, some of them carrying a weapon, some of them carrying an axe. There have been instances when people -- civilians said, I am staying close to you. If you get killed in the battle, I'll get your weapon and fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during this time after May 9th, were -- was there any -- was there any digging of trenches, any building of fortifications, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe that.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. Initially from the asphalt side of the road, we tried to take up a position. Then we -- from our positions, we went to the other positions, meaning that we communicated with each other in the two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to show you this later, but maybe I should show you now. 9

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could have image 8 from P1. On the ELMO, please. That's good I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did I show you this photograph yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you want, it may be easier, you can look to your left. Not on the computer screen but to your left. You can see the picture there. Could you -- do you recognise where this place is in the photo?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: This is in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can, see if you can, find the positions you were just telling us about. You talked about after May 9th you started building fortifications and there were two positions which communicated with each other. Can you point to where those positions were.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I can't see them very clearly here because it's an aerial image. It's hard for me to define [as interpreted] it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, take your time to look at it and see if you can find them. Do you see the Peja-Pristina road on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I can't see very clearly -- yes, I can see the Peja-Pristina road. Initially the fighting was taking place here approximately, because as I said I cannot see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So is the area you were just pointing out one of the positions you were telling us about that were established?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I'm not clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The question is -- and maybe you can't do it, but you talked about two positions after May 9th that communicated with each other when fortifications were being built. Can you find either of those two positions on the aerial photo?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I'm not clear about the two points. I am talking about the second day, about the 9th of May. But after the 9th of May the positions that I spoke about, the trenches, I cannot tell them here. I cannot find them here, the place where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not able to indicate on this photo where the trenches were dug?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It's not that I do not want to, but I cannot find them in the map, in this terrain that I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we can remove that for now and we'll probably look at it a little bit later. Now, when did the digging of trenches begin?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: When you mean? The time when? On the next day, everybody started to build a trench for himself, to dig his own trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long did that go on for? How long were people digging trenches after May 9th?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: As I said, everybody started to dig a trench for himself. I answered this question that initially everybody dug up a position for himself, for a single person. Then we dig more -- dug more -- dug more in order for these trenches to communicate with one another, for the soldiers to pass on from one to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And approximately how long did this activity take? In other words, how long were people digging trenches after May 9th in order to allow soldiers to communicate and pass from one to the other?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't remember how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember how far these trenches extended, how long they were?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: You mean between one another -- among each other or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. What was the length of the trenches between the points?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: They were very close to one another. Maybe 10, 15 metres one from the other, that was the distance because we were few soldiers in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many soldiers approximately were present in Lapusnik at this time just after the battle of May 9th?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: We were around 12, 13. I can't give you an exact number. It was approximately that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after this date, did the amount of soldiers increase, decrease, or stay the same in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I said a little bit earlier that the number changed on a daily basis, because many people came asking to join the KLA. But as I said when I spoke about Drenica, we were there -- were in the same situation having in a day 10, 12, more soldiers -- people wanting to join us. We didn't have enough weapons to give them. We had only enough weapons for ourselves. Some civilians came there, some of them carried their own weapons, ammunitions, some of them came with axes, as I said. Just because they wanted to join, we couldn't tell them to stay or to leave because there was not enough munitions, as I said. Those who had arms, joined -- could stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was -- how long did Voglushi remain in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Until he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: He was killed -- he died a heroic death on the 26th of July, 1998. Many of us maybe wanted to have the same fate, to die heroically like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was he a good soldier?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: He was a very good soldier. He was of a heavy build. He had a strong voice. He was, as we said to [as interpreted] him, the lion of Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said "we said of him." Is that the way the other soldiers in Lapusnik thought of him not just you? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: We called him "Voglushi," but this is what -- we looked upon him as being the lion of Lapusnik, as a brave, very brave person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was his position in Lapusnik after May 9th?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Initially he was one of us, a soldier, because there was not any command organisation there. There was no one to lead us. He was a soldier just like all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said "initially he was one of us, a soldier just like all of us." Did his position change over time?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. Seeing that he was -- he enjoyed the respect of all of us, he was from Komorane, from Bushat village, he knew the terrain. The people knew him and respected him greatly. We -- therefore, we, all of us, the comrades there who felt the need to have someone in the leadership, someone to be as the leader of our unit, we decided to elect him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what kind of leader was he in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: After our proposal we asked him to lead us since he knew the terrain very well. The people knew him, he enjoyed great authority in that region. So we asked him whether he was willing to be our leader, to show us the way and such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you now about the 18th of May and whether there was fighting in Lapusnik on that date.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember exactly the date. I am not sure whether it was 18th or the 19th. There was fighting between us and the Serb paramilitary forces. The fighting was very severe. It lasted until the 10th or 11th p.m. [as interpreted]. They the Serb forces wanted to know whether we were still there. They wanted to sound out the situation, so they attempted to penetrate again the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I saw you just wincing for a moment, sir, and I know that you suffer still from your injuries. So please let me know if you don't feel well, if you feel ill, if you need a break, anything like that. I know it's sometimes difficult for you to stand or sit.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It was difficult for me even during the war. But despite our pains, despite the injuries we have suffered, we want to testify here to the truth, to the reality that we know of. This pain is with me constantly, but I can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just let me know if you need --

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: If you think we can have a break, of course, like all -- we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll probably take one in about 15 minutes, but if you're in pain or if you don't feel well at any time, just let me know and we can probably take a break early.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please describe in a little bit more detail the attack on Lapusnik by the Serb forces that you were just talking about. What type of weaponry did they employ if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Of course I remember. All kinds of weapons. They used all kinds of weapons. In the beginning, they did not use rockets but they used mines and shelling and all kinds of weapons. There were -- there was fighting there. We were in the defence line. We were defending the population from the Serbs, and they were shelling us from far away with rockets and mortars and whatever they had at their disposal. They used all of their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you defend yourselves? What weapons did you have and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: The reality is that you cannot believe what kinds of weapons we had and what kinds of weapons we used to defend ourselves. They had modern weapons, while we had light weapons. But fortunately, because God was on our side, God saved us. Because the weaponry we had -- the weaponry they had was so heavy, it is unbelievable that we had only two casualties, two people who died. It's completely -- it takes me -- it takes my breath away when I think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at this battle, around the 18th of May, how many KLA soldiers were there in Lapusnik fighting back against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. It might have been 20 of us, plus/minus three of us, three soldiers. I can't say precisely how many soldiers there were. It's been a long time since the war, and we've had a lot of difficulties since the war. So I can't remember all the things. And in fact, after the war I wanted to forget everything about it because when I went home I could see the houses burnt down, the people who were killed. I didn't want to remember all those bad things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And following on from the 18th of May after this battle, you talked about how after the 9th of May villagers came and people came to try to help. Following the 18th of May battle, what happened to the numbers of soldiers in Lapusnik? Did it grow, shrink, remain the same?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I responded to this earlier. The number of the members of the KLA increased every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as these numbers increased, were any other soldiers -- any other leaders, excuse me, selected by the soldiers in addition to Voglushi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the time frame, say, the weeks after 18 May 1998.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I don't remember the exact time, but several weeks after the 18th of May Voglushi proposed Qerqizi - his pseudonym was Qerqizi - because he looked like Qerqiz Topulli, one of the Albanian fighters against the Turks, Osmanli Turks. And Ymer proposed in our presence, he said that, This person can lead us properly. And we agreed. We supported his idea, Ymer's idea, because Ymer was the person responsible for us at that moment and we thought as Ymer proposed him, he knows him, so it's the right decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was Qerqizi's real name?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was the first time you met Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether it was the first day or the second day, I mean the 9th of May. I can't remember exactly whether it was the 8th or the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long was Isak Musliu, Qerqizi, in Lapusnik while you were there?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: All the time [as interpreted]. He was all the time in Lapusnik [as interpreted] until the battle when the gorge fell, but then he went to other villages, to Rahovec, to Fustica. He went there to help with other soldiers of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be very clear, the battle when the gorge fell is 26th July 1998?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what kind of a leader was Qerqizi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Qerqizi was our leader. We needed somebody to lead us so that we would not be an army of vagabonds or people who are not organised. We needed somebody to be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you personally feel about it once Isak Musliu had become in charge?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Everybody felt good because we wanted this army to take the form or the shape or -- of a real army, of a full, a complete army. And we had to know who to look up to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a couple minutes early; I think maybe the witness would not mind a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have our first break now, resuming at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've just asked for the witness to remain out of court. I've raised this with Mr. Nicholls and we both think that it is appropriate that he should remain out while I raise a matter on the transcript. Could I draw your attention to line 13 at page 25. Our interpreter heard the words after the words "all the time," which now reads "full stop, He was all the time in Lapusnik." Our interpreter heard the words "apart from when he went to Rahovec to help." Now, we will listen to the tapes overnight. This is of something of particular significance in the case of Musliu, and therefore we thought it appropriate to raise it in a slightly equivocal manner at the moment until we've been definitively able to listen to the tapes and, we hope the Court would agree, more appropriate to raise it absent the witness. I don't know if Mr. Nicholls wants to go back over this point at this stage or not. It's a matter for him, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, thank you for that. I think it was properly raised in the absence of the witness. Subject to anything Mr. Nicholls wants to say; he shows no signs of needing to say anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the idea of having the tape checked overnight is the practical course to take to see whether there is or is not something that needs clarifying. If we could have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just before the break you were telling us about how you felt when Isak Musliu became a leader. After that in June and July, how often did you see him in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: He stayed all the time there with us. He helped us a lot. He gave us courage, and very often he used the words "it's God that has given us the soil, not the Serbs." And when we were fighting, he would sing together with Ymer. They were fighting and singing and that's what gave us courage. We became stronger when we heard them singing in the midst of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so just to be clear, during this time when he was in Lapusnik in June and July all the time, did you see him on a daily basis, weekly, or how often did you actually see him in person?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what part of Lapusnik was he a leader of or in charge of? All of it or part of it? Can you describe the area.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. He was only in the part where we were, because there were several units in Lapusnik. There was Guri, Pellumbi, Lumi, ourselves. He was responsible only for the narrower part of Lapusnik, the narrower point of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is that on the same side of the road, the Pristina-Pec road that you were telling us about earlier, on the left side heading towards Peja?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you've talked about the names of some units, Guri, Pellumbi. If you remember, what was the name of the unit that Qerqiz was responsible for, your unit?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Our unit was called Celiku. During the first fightings on the 8th and the 9th of May, we felt very strong, like steel; that's why we were called Celik, because of that. Celik means steel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's explanation, Celik means steel; the last part was interpreter's explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did your unit also have a number?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: During that period -- in fact, it was Celiku 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just tell me where the other units you've mentioned were. The Pellumbi, Guri, and Lumi, where were they stationed?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. At the edge of our position, there was Guri and Pellumbi on the right. There was the Pristina-Peja road; on the right of that was Guri and Pellumbi. I'm not sure but the Pellumbi unit was under us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you mean that the Pellumbi unit was under you?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: One Pellumbi unit was below our area. It was a hilly area, so at the bottom there is a place called Komorane -- Kishna Reka/Komorane. There was a Pellumbi unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me find a map for you and we'll see if you can mark approximately where these units were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Look at that map for a moment, sir, that's map 6 from P1. And I have not shown you that map before, have I?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can, could you just look at that map and see if you can see where the relative positions were of Celiku 3, the Pellumbis, Guri and Lumi units.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: In the places I touched, there were the units Guri, Pellumbi in the places I'm going to show now. Guri, Pellumbi, and Lumi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have the witness be given a pen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you just mark with a "P" where the Pellumbi units were.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness has marked what looks like a P next to Kishna Reka. Maybe if we could give the witness a ballpoint pen it might be easier for him to write it. We have one over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you please mark with a "G" where the Guri units were.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's legible. Sorry, if we can give you a better pen. And can you mark with an "L" where the Lumi units were.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I am writing these letters down approximately because I can't say exactly where they were. But in the Lapusnik area, these were the units that were active there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you also mark a "C" where your Celiku 3 unit was stationed.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I thought earlier when you were talking about the Pellumbi units you were showing a range where those units were stationed. Is there anywhere else where that Pellumbi units -- you remember being stationed?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood earlier. I thought you were pointing to a different place where there were also Pellumbi units. And can you tell me, where you've marked the P by Kishna Reka, is that the only place you remember the Pellumbi unit being stationed or were they anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No. This was part of Pellumbi, but there were Pellumbi units beyond the asphalt road. But I did not have direct contact with them. But I know that beyond the asphalt road there was Guri, Pellumbi unit, and Lumi. So where I put the P letter, there's where the Pellumbi unit I knew was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what you mean beyond the asphalt road is these other units is the other side of the Pristina-Peja highway. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Other than the Celiku 3 unit you've marked and the Pellumbi unit you've marked on the south side of the Pristina-Peja highway, were there any other KLA units in this area operating during May, June, July 1998?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I'm not clear -- well, as far as I know, these were the ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to give that a number and admit it, Your Honour. I'm not sure which number we're up to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be Prosecution Exhibit P127.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you on another topic now. Do you know a man named Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I remember this person on the first days of the fighting. I can't remember exactly which date, but possibly the first fightings on the 18th and 19th of May. And he said, I want to go to Korretice to take my family away from that area because it's dangerous there. I will take my family to Bajice. I did not see him from that time on, and I thought he had been killed or anything like that. But after that I heard he had been somewhere in Luznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now just to be clear, you say "on the first days of the fighting," and then you talk about on the 18th and 19th of May that you had a conversation with Haradin Bala. Is the first day that you met Haradin Bala the first day of the fighting on the 18th and 19th of May or on the 8th and 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I said earlier that the first -- it was the first days of fighting. There were several fightings that went on there at that period. I remember one time when a helicopter came to observe us whether we were there or not, and there was shelling every day. But I have seen this person from the first days until the 18th or the 19th, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So does that mean you saw him for about ten days?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Haradin Bala have a pseudonym when you knew him in May 1998?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. He must have had, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember -- well, would it help you to look at your statement? Would it help you to remember?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't need to see it, but as I am saying -- I don't have any documents here with me because I have solemnly declared here that I will Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tell the truth. And I don't need the statements because I will only tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that you're here to tell the truth and that you are -- what I mean is that you spoke about a pseudonym for Haradin Bala in your July 2003 statement, and you've told me you were truthful when you gave that statement. I was wondering if it would help you to remember to look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I take it from that that Mr. Nicholls is attempting to lead the witness to an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I'm attempting to refresh his recollection. It's a topic which has come --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, then he's done it in a totally improper fashion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've had an answer from the witness, Mr. Nicholls, that he doesn't need to see the statement. So I think perhaps you better move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wasn't sure that the witness knew the document we were talking about, because he said he didn't have any documents with him. I wanted to make it clear to him that I was talking about his ICTY statement and whether that might help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he says he knows what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during those ten days how often did you see Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I could say regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I say "regularly" because there were not thousands of us there; there were only 20 or 22 soldiers during that period that we're talking about. So there were not too many of us. It's probable that on a certain day I did not see him, but I can say that I saw him every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where would you see him in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I saw him where we were staying because in the beginning we stayed around the asphalt road - we were sleeping there - and every day when we were guards and we saw him when we stayed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what were his duties during the time you knew him in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: The same as myself: Observe the terrain. There was a checkpoint in Komorane which was 200 or 300 metres [as interpreted] as the crow flies away from us, and we had to observe the area if forces were coming our way, how many forces were coming our way. All the tasks that we had all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we'll talk about that later, your tasks. Just to be clear, the checkpoint in Komorane, was that a Serb or a KLA checkpoint that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It was a Serbian checkpoint, of course, of the Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after the last time you saw Haradin Bala in Lapusnik - you might have answered this, I'm not sure - which was the next time you saw him again or did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for interjecting, but these things often are easier to sort out at the earliest opportunity. I believe again there appears to be an error on the LiveNote. I understand that the witness's answer was not "200 or 300 metres as the crow flies." It was 2 or 3 kilometres between the point and Komorane. Your Honour, perhaps that can be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's another matter perhaps for overnight, Mr. Khan. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I can ask the witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, was the checkpoint at Komorane 200 or 300 metres or -- you heard the question, or 2 or 3 kilometres? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Approximately 2 kilometres and 2 or 300 metres. I couldn't measure it exactly, of course, because I did not have the means to, but 2 kilometres and 2 or 300 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And the question I asked you before Mr. Khan stood up was: Did you see Haradin Bala again after he left Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I see -- I saw him in Bajice sometime around the new year 1998/1999, and when I saw him I was joking with him: I thought you were killed. I thought you had deserted. And he said, Well, no, no, but I suffer -- I have a heart condition and I have this permission to go and stay with my family. That's where I saw him in this period and then also when I saw him before, during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did you hear that he'd been in Luznica?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I heard it from him because I asked him, Did you desert the army or were you killed? And he said, No, I am serving in Luznica but our commander gave me permission to leave, temporarily leave, to stay with my family for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to move on to another topic now. You talked about sleeping at the fighting positions by the asphalt road when you first arrived at Lapusnik. Later on were you able to sleep and stay somewhere more comfortable indoors?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where was that? Where did you stay later after you weren't sleeping outside?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: In the beginning we stayed at our positions, but the population of the village came and took us. We left two or three guards while the others went to sleep to the -- at the houses of the villagers. They gave us tea and food and prepared water for cleaning, for us to clean ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was Gzim Gashi? Do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. He was a villager from Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you ever stay in his -- on his property?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was that, what period?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Sometime around the end, before the Lapusnik gorge fell. I stayed in the oda of Gezim Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you stay there for the whole -- well, for how long before Lapusnik gorge fell?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: You mean how long did I stay there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. A month? A week? How long did you stay in Gezim Gashi's place?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but maybe a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did other KLA soldiers stay there with you?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: About how many?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I did not hear it very well, the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How many soldiers approximately stayed in Gezim Gashi's place, his property, during that last month when you were there?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: The number of soldiers changed constantly. Sometimes there were three soldiers, sometimes five, sometimes seven, another time two. So there was not a constant number of soldiers staying there in that oda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph now, that's U003-4901.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we can put it on Sanction and we can also perhaps put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Look at the photograph for a moment, Mr. Karpuzi.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you see a signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document from seeing it before?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. During questioning by Ole Lehtinen, the investigator, he showed me this photograph, and my signature is here as well as Lehtinen's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that during your interview on -- in July 2003?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. But at that time the photograph was bigger and it was clearer than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And also I showed you the photograph yesterday, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You see the markings, the words written in Albanian, around the outside of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who made those markings, those labels, of different places?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And what is the place we see in this photograph? What is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Ole, when he showed me this photograph, he asked me whether I recognised this terrain; and I said, Yes. After he asked me questions about a prison in Lapusnik, he said that the prison was here; and I said to him that, I don't know anything about it but I can tell you that I've stayed in this area myself. This is Gezim's house, and everything is marked there, what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's just go through the markings which you made, and I hope everybody has a translation. Perhaps it's on the -- it's a bit difficult to see on the computer screen for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Nicholls. I wonder if I could ask him to be - and I know he will want to be - careful. Putting this in front of the witness and asking him the question at the line 22: "What is the place we see in this photograph?" That presupposes that is one place. I say no more in the presence of the witness, but I would ask Mr. Nicholls to proceed with his customary caution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at the first notation you've written on the top right of the page, on the top right corner of the photograph, what have you written there?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: The kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And whose kitchen was that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: This was Gzim's kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you ever go into that kitchen yourself?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the kitchen -- you've labelled it as the kitchen, but what was the kitchen used for at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: We had food there, we ate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And the next building on the right you've labelled as well. Could you tell us what that building is that you've drawn an arrow to.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the one you've labelled "Gzim's house." Could you describe that building, what that was used for.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It was used by Gzim's family, but later - I mean, while I was staying there - we cleaned ourselves in that house, what you call a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in addition to washing there, did you do anything else there?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever stay there?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It is on the same yard, and I don't understand what you mean, Have you stayed there? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's okay. I understand that you used that place for washing, that house. Okay. And below that you've written "the oda of Gzim Vojvoda." Can you describe --

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe what that building is.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: This is what we call an oda, and it is used for men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think you said earlier that you slept there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what's written there in your handwriting is "oda of Gzim Vojvoda," and is that correct, the last name? Is it Gzim Vojvoda or is it Gzim Gashi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: His name was Gzim Gashi, but they are from Llapi and they are called Vojvoda or Shalajns. That's how we called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever do any kind of work in Gzim's compound?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Could you explain it to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, in addition to sleeping there and washing there and eating there, I wonder if you ever had any tasks there, any kind of duties there.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you describe those, please.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I kept documentation, lists of the soldiers, because we had to know where the soldiers were from, in order, for example, when they got killed or got wounded, we would know who they were and where they were from.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have one of the mikes of the witness turned on, please; it's gone off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll ask you some questions about that record-keeping later. But where in Gzim's compound were those records kept which you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: In Gzim's oda. The records that I kept about the soldiers, I kept them in the oda. There was not too much space or too much room to keep things. I kept them in the oda; that's -- there's where I kept them. They were not secret documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we move down on the right side you've written "the house of Bali Vojvoda," and there is an arrow pointing to the house, the same house or building which is labelled number 3. Can you describe what that building was used for.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: There were some soldiers staying there, too. We had to stay as few soldiers as possible in one single place in case of shelling. When a shell might fall there in one place, we saw to it that there were as few victims as possible. That's why we kept a small number of soldiers in one single place, to ensure a small number of victims if that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever enter this house, the house of Bali Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what would you do in that house?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: During our free time when we were not doing anything, when there was no fighting, we stayed there with our friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about the soldiers who were staying there, would they ever cross the road to Gzim's compound and come into the oda?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we continue to the labels which you've drawn on the bottom of the photograph. The first one is to a building which is labelled 2B and you've drawn an arrow to it and labelled it as the "cowshed." Can you tell me what this building -- what that little shed was used for.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, the owner of this house, in that place he used to keep his cows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever go into that cowshed?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever enter the compound which we see there, which the cowshed is part of? I'll withdraw that question; that's a really bad question. The next label to the left which you've made is not labelled with any number but it's written "bunari," the well. I think that's self-explanatory. Is there anything -- any comment you have to make on the well?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I know that there was a well there. We got water from that well. I don't know what to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And continuing around the left side of the page you've drawn an arrow to a white building which is marked with the number 2. And you've written "oda of ?" Can you tell you about that building. What was that building used for?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: That building was used for the soldiers to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know who owned this compound, the one we're now talking about where you've written "the oda of ?" Do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the owner. I know that he was an old old [as interpreted], an old man, short. I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. The building on the left side of the photo marked number 1, you haven't written anything about that building. Did you ever enter that building?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, speaking about the oda, building number 2, how often did you visit that building? Let's say in July now.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I can't give you an accurate estimate of how often I've been there, but I do know that I've been there several times. I've stayed in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say "the room, the oda," is that upstairs or downstairs?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: What do you mean upstairs and downstairs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In the building marked number 2, if you remember, was the oda upstairs, that's a two-storey house, or downstairs, on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: When you enter it from the street it was on the right side. It was I think the second floor now, come to think of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what would you do in the oda there with the other soldiers? Can you just describe what that room was used for?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Often after the fighting -- there was a television set there. So after the fighting we were there to watch television. In our free time we got together, we used to sing -- some of us used to sing. We listened to them. We kind of built up some courage in those hard days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, in the compound which building 2 is part of, the building with the oda that you've told us you used to watch television in, did you enter ever any other buildings in that compound?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: There was an antechamber and a chamber, otherwise oda; I've been there many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But other than the building the oda is in and the house, did you go to any other buildings in the compound, detached buildings?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't have so much free time. We were not there in a wedding. I remember very well that, as I said, I've been in that oda many times. We sang, we drank tea, we watched television. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Haradin Bala in the oda we're speaking about in the building marked number 2?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about the Isak Musliu? Did you ever see him in the oda?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, he used to sing together with Ymer Alushani and some other comrades. Qerqizi sang, Ymer, and some other who knew how to sing and to play instruments. They used to sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
