utterances.text: Did you ever see any persons other than KLA soldiers in this compound that we're talking about, the compound across from Gzim Gashi's, across the road from Gzim Gashi's compound?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: What do you mean? What are you talking about? Which compound do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the compound with the oda you would stay in and sing songs in which is marked as building number 2 and you've marked as "the oda of," you didn't remember the name. Did you see any civilians in this compound ever?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you -- I know the numbers fluctuated, you made that point. But can you give me an approximate number of how many soldiers would stay in this compound?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I said even earlier that the number varied. In none of the houses there was an accurate number, a definite number. We had to change locations because I don't know how the Serb force knew, but it so happened that every time we were in a house the Serbs used to shell that particular house. That's why we used to change places. So I have no idea how many soldiers were situated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to talk about another topic. We can leave the document with you for the moment. While you were in Lapusnik in May, June, or July of 1998, did you ever take an oath as a KLA soldier?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember about when that was?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't remember accurately whether it was end of June or after -- or early July. This I don't remember. During the time I gave the statement, I already pointed that out. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. That's fine. I'd like -- where did that -- where did that oath -- where did you take that oath?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. The place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where were you physically when you made this oath as a KLA soldier?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: We took the oath in the yard of Bali's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And -- thank you. Could you look at that diagram to your left now and see if you can see the place. You said "the yard of Bali." Does that appear on the photograph? So if you could just point that out on the photograph to your left on the ELMO if you see the place where the ceremony took place.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It is not in the photo. It is approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We couldn't see that. Could you just -- maybe if we make the photograph smaller. A little bit more. Now, Mr. Karpuzi, if you could try to point out where the ceremony took place.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: It is approximately, as I said, here because it doesn't show in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could I give the witness -- have the witness be given a pen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just mark with an "X" the location you've just indicated, the approximate location of the oath ceremony.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Since it's not in the picture it's outside, approximately -- can I do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. If you think you can show where it should be if we had a larger photograph.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the witness has made an X just to the top left corner of the number 3 box on the photograph. And I'd ask that it be admitted at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit P128.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now to tell me as much as you can about what you remember from the oath ceremony. And I'll start off with -- you said earlier that "we took the oath in the yard." How many soldiers took the oath that day?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact figure. Must have been 50, 60 soldiers. As far as I could estimate with my eye, 50, 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you take part in the oath ceremony at all, other than taking the oath? Did you perform any actions as part of the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I'm sorry. Put it in a simple form, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Describe the oath ceremony in your words. What happened when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I saw Ymeri calling all of us out and he even joked, Come on, guys, we have to get together. We went there. It was the flag in a mast, and together with the two soldiers we raised the flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And Ymeri, is that Voglushi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the transcript says "together with two soldiers we raised the flag," that's what I was asking. Did you participate in raising the flag?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yeah, I said what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember if Isak Musliu was present?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I think yes. I am not sure because a long time has passed, but to my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you remember who administered the oath or how the oath was administered?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: When the investigator asked me, I clearly indicated that when we went there there was this line of 50, 60 soldiers. We entered the line. I asked Ymer, Can I please raise the flag because my father -- because of the flag he was sentenced, so can I do that? He said, Yes, you can. So we raised the flag. Someone read the text of the oath, and we repeated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I know that you've answered these questions when you were asked by the investigator, but I need to ask some of the same ones again here in court.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember the text of the oath or the words of the oath that you made?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were there any speeches during the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: There were no speeches. I said even earlier that there was not any formal speech given. I don't remember the name of Commander Celiku. There was no Commander Celiku as far as I know at that time, but among the soldiers there was one called Celik. And he told us, Guys, we are fighting for Kosova, and that we must defend the people by all means. We Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have to shed the last drop of our blood for the people, all the people. This was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this Celiku who made a short speech, had you ever seen him before?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you talk about anything else?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember talking about the speech when you gave your statement in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a cautionary word. Of course my learned friend knows what's coming next. But the witness has already said he spoke to the Prosecution prior to giving evidence today. He has had an opportunity to look at statements, and of course what Your Honours are interested in hearing is the witness's recollection of what happened. So I would point to my learned friend to be careful on this issue; he would be familiar, of course, with the point I'm making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember talking about this short speech given by Celiku when you made your statement to the investigator in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my objection stands. What's important is what's said to have happened at that speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's nothing improper in that question, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the ground of relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything may come from it. We will proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can answer the question, Mr. Karpuzi. Do you remember if you talked about that short speech when you made your statement to the Prosecution investigator in 2003?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I already told you what was said in that speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know. The question is: Do you remember talking about it to the investigator in 2003 when you made your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember what you told the investigator in 2003? Just if you remember it.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I already said -- told you the words that were mentioned in what you call a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me just ask you if you think it would be helpful at all to refresh your memory to look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't have any statements with me here, and I already answered your question I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a slightly different one. I have a copy of your statement in Albanian. The question is if you think it would help you to remember to look at that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, one can take a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Khan. I'm ahead of you. I'm just poised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would it help you to look at your statement to remember?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't think it would help. I don't need to see the statement when I know what I'm saying. I already explained to you that there was not such, as you are referring to, a speech. But it was a friendly, informal talk. We are the sons of the people, he said. I think I mentioned that before. I believe I am clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And was this person Celiku, who made the statement, introduced in any way to the soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't remember. He introduced himself. Someone among the soldiers said, This guy is Celiku, but he was not introduced as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, had you heard of Celiku before?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Never before?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the soldiers present to this short statement by Celiku?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: The soldiers welcomed this talk, this conversation, but among the comrades there were some who began to joke when he said, We are the sons of the people and that we must be careful with the civilians irrespective of the ethnicity or whether -- whoever they are. All of them have to be treated equally among us. There were some who said, What, are we going to treat the Serbs like all the other Kosovars? They were making fun of his words. He said, I don't want to accept this duty -- because we asked him to assume responsibility. This is what you asked me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're getting there to what I asked you about, yes. How did you personally react to his speech -- to his statement?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I don't remember how I responded personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you said that some people made fun of his words about treating everybody equally. Did you think that that was a good idea or -- okay. So what I'm asking is if you supported or did not support those statements made by Celiku about treating civilians well, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, who asked him, Celiku, to assume responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: We, the soldiers. We asked him to lead us after that talk. We asked him, Can you please lead us because you have a good communication skill, you know how to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: After the words he told us -- after hearing the soldiers retorting to his words, he refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever learn Celiku's real name?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: At that time -- afterwards, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you learn Celiku's real name?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I learned his true name sometime after the brigades were formed. It was then when I heard -- learned his true name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what name did you learn was Celiku's true name?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Fatmir Limaj was Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the oath ceremony where Celiku was asked to be a leader, did you see him again in Lapusnik before the 26th of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes, during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During which fighting?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: There was frequent fighting going on there. I have seen him two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what were you doing when you saw him those different times?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I was on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was Fatmir Limaj doing when he visited you or you saw him on the front line?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: He was fighting alongside us. Can I make an explanation, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: At a period during the fighting they called him uncle, "daja," in Albanian. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's your -- okay. And the two or three times when you saw Fatmir Limaj between the oath ceremony and the 26th of July. You say "he was fighting alongside us." Is that on each occasion?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how much time did you spend fighting alongside Limaj, Fatmir Limaj, on those dates?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I'm not clear. What do you mean how long? During a day of fighting or altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. I'm sorry the question wasn't clear. When you saw Fatmir Limaj on those occasions, how long did you see him for on each of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: During one fighting, I remember seeing him that day. It might have lasted two, three hours, or a whole day that he was among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him when you were not fighting, when you were not in actual combat in Lapusnik after the oath ceremony?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the oath ceremony, were there any other leaders selected the way you've described Voglushi and Isak Musliu being selected to be leaders?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: To my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Celiku referred to as anything other than an ordinary soldier?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember accurately, it was September, October, or November, I heard him being referred to as a commander of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which area?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Of Brigade 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which units made up Brigade 121?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: All the small groups that were there -- from Kizhareke, Nekovce, Bajice, Shale, Kroimire, Pjetershtice, Carraleve, up to Luzhnice -- all these merged into Brigade 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just if you can remember, can you remember the names of those units which merged and became the Brigade 121, not just the locations?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember because I was not in each and every one of them for me to know their names. This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You've talked about Celiku 3. Do you know if that became part of the 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: Yes. Celiku 3, after the Lapusnik gorge battle the soldiers dispersed. It was an initiative taken for every one of them to go to their own respective villages where they were familiar with the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's about five minutes early. Would it be a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume just after a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Karpuzi, let me just ask you a few more questions going back to the oath ceremony, which you said was in late June or early July 1998. Now, after that oath ceremony before the 26th of July, 1998, during that period of time did you ever hear of Celiku referred to as Commander Celiku?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You stated that at the oath ceremony he was asked to be a leader and he stated he was not prepared to be a leader. At any point during that oath ceremony did he change his mind? Did he later state that he would be prepared to be a leader of the soldiers in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So just so I'm clear, the only thing he said about his willingness to be a leader the whole time was that he was not willing to be a leader?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I explained even earlier the reasons why he said, I'm not prepared to be a leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And my question is, just to be clear, is that was his consistent position the entire time?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: I didn't stay all the time with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're talking about during the oath ceremony.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: During the oath ceremony, after the oath -- the oath all lasted one, two minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That day of the oath ceremony at any point did Celiku state that he was willing to be a leader?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've sat down for as long as I could contain myself. Your Honour, perhaps it shows how little patience I have, but I've tried. Your Honour, my friend has asked a number of questions which amount to leading questions. He knows how to conduct examination-in-chief, and the witness of course has said -- he was asked to describe the events of the oath ceremony, and he has done that. And I would ask that Your Honours guide my friend in relation to what is permissible and that which is not. I hate to keep interrupting court proceedings in the manner that, unfortunately, I feel that I have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. The Chamber will not give any guidance of this nature. The answer given at the beginning was clear. I would understand Mr. Nicholls to be making quite clear that the full import of the question was understood by the witness so that his answer is not subject to qualification at some later point, so that on that basis this is being allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I just add that it is an issue where there are difficulties because of translation and because of evident difficulties in getting this and other witnesses to understand questions which to you and I might seem clear and convey one thing, but apparently to others convey something different. And for that reason, some greater liberty is being shown than would be perhaps with an English-speaking witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I hope in all of this sight is not being lost of fundamental truth and don't be too worried about the implications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You probably need me to ask that again, the question again, Witness. I'm talking about the day of the oath ceremony. At any point during the day of the oath ceremony did Celiku state that he would be prepared to be a leader, that he would accept to be a leader?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: No. I explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be very clear, between the date of the oath ceremony and the 26th of July did Celiku ever agree to be a leader?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: This I don't know. I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would it help you to look at your statement perhaps, where you talk about this issue? If you're having trouble remembering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know I am telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know you're telling me what you know but you just stated in response to the last question that you didn't remember. If I wonder if you looked at your statement where the situation was raised if it would help you to remember, if you think it would help you to remember.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI
utterances.text: If you deem it appropriate, you might bring me a copy of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know what you are at the moment proposing to do, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was proposing to give him a copy of his statement because I understood the answer to be that if it's appropriate he would look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis should the witness see that statement at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To refresh his recollection of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And on what basis can he refresh a recollection by a statement made some five years after the event?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because he -- perhaps we should send the witness out, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not. I'm asking you a question of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, because five years after the event is closer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Three years. Well, the statement is in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Five years. It's closer in time, obviously, to now -- than we are today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let's go back to refreshing recollection, simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If he believes it may help him remember, he may be refreshed with anything, including his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that your proposition of law?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not the view taken by the Chamber. It can't be refreshed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the witness feels it would help him to remember to look at that statement, a statement he's made, signed, stated as true, and reviewed, then on that basis he should be allowed to review the statement. And that's -- sorry, the practice I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any authority to support that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't have it at my fingertips, but this is the way I would lay the foundation back home is to ask the witness if the statement would help him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think it's another area where there may be some divergence between some jurisdictions that have an adversarial system. The common-law rule of which I am aware is that refreshment of recollection can be on the basis of a statement or more often notes, but a statement made whilst the memory is fresh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not the -- that would be perhaps a past recollection recorded or a contemporaneous recording. However, refreshing recollection in my practice is different. It does not need to be contemporaneous. It can be anything which helps to trigger the memory of the witness. So you may have a witness that has gone over things, and feels that it would help him. It does not need to be contemporaneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I can only say that that's not something familiar to me, the basis upon which you say this Tribunal proceeds, and you can bring that to the attention of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry I don't have case law at my fingertips about refreshing recollection here. But in other cases, many times in a previous trial I was in, I was -- it was accepted to refresh the witness's memory when it would be helpful to the witness with his statement which was invariably made years after the events in question. So it's not foreign to my practice here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps just to assist I would make simply one comment, with your leave, which I hope would be of some assistance. Even apart from the comments which Your Honour has very usefully put forward, the starting point in my submission would also be that the witness has had an opportunity to refresh his memory from these documents because that was what precisely was done in proofing with members of the Office of the Prosecution. So he has had an opportunity to refresh his memory. And what you want to hear, Your Honours, collectively, is the witness's statement as to the true events that occurred rather than of course the Prosecution seeking to give a meaning to a statement recorded over two days at which you can't see the questions that were asked. Your Honour, that's the only comment I seek to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Khan, while you're on your feet, you may be able to assist the Chamber. Is there any practice with which you're familiar of this Tribunal which would support the position taken by Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the starting point I think of course and Rule 89 of the Rules that the Trial Chambers will devise is simply those that would best assist the fair determination of a matter. I think the starting point of course -- testimony is not supposed to be a memory test. It would in my submission be not impermissible for a witness to read a statement even if it was made years after the event prior to giving testimony if it is thought that it would assist him in telling the true facts. Your Honour, of course this statement is given five years after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't question that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it is usual practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question then in the course of giving evidence and being able to turn to that is the issue that confronts us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course there is decisions from this Trial Chambers and others -- perhaps if I have a moment I could get the decisions, but when one says that they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are they -- I'm trying to be educated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps you're looking at the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the same proposition, in my submission, would apply as a matter of logic that if testimony is not to be a test of memory it shouldn't be simply the practice to put an investigator's statement that's finally signed by a witness to a witness in order to get him to say something; what you want to hear, of course, is the witness's recollection of the events. Your Honours, on the specific question as to case law, my understanding is quite different from my learned friend's, that the Prosecution can't willy-nilly and put previous statements to witnesses, absent to showing it is necessary. And that is extremely onerous, in my submission, when the Prosecution have already had an opportunity but a day before to go through previous statements with a witness and to proof him. In my submission, it's totally unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Khan. Does any other counsel wish to add anything at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour, briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm seeing if I can assist you, but it's taking me a little time to wade through the various potentially relevant paragraphs. Would Your Honours bear with me as I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As counsel can appreciate, the members of the Chamber are always willing to be informed of practice as it has developed in this Tribunal with which we may not be familiar immediately. That's why I'm allowing these submissions. And while you're looking, Mr. Topolski, I think Mr. Nicholls may have something he wishes to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour, from what I think my friend was trying to say, that is not -- his argument has nothing to do with refreshing recollection. Refreshing recollection is not having the witness parrot what is in the statement. It has got nothing to do with what he remembered and what he reviewed in a statement at an early time. The purpose is not to have the witness do anything other than testify to the best of his memory, the best that he remembers the truth. So the fact that he has reviewed his statement yesterday, which is true, should not bar his being able to look at it again if it were to assist just in some way for him to remember, from his own memory, what happened. The purpose is not to have him read what is in the statement but simply to use the statement as a tool to remember certain things. I can just say on one occasion when I previously ask him he did later remember and say exactly what was in his statement. So it may help him to clear up this matter which is material, I think, if he looks at his statement. Now, of course the instruction to him is not, Read what is in the statement and say it, or That's true, isn't it? The question is, Read this paragraph, see if it helps you to remember. And the start of all this, the witness said he wasn't sure if he didn't remember something relating to the specific point about accepting a command. So what Your Honours will hear, he may say that it helps or it doesn't help. But what the testimony will be will be his memory. Mr. Khan said it's not to be a memory test, a trial, and that is exactly right, which is why if a witness has some difficulty remembering something on the stand which he could remember with a bit of help either from a statement, a book, and audio clip, anything, if that may help him remember, that may help the Chamber receive evidence. And I may have a citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do have a citation which may be of assistance. It's an appeals decision from Hadzihasanovic from the 2nd of April, 2004. I haven't read the decision, but I believe it supports the position I'm taking that witnesses, at least here, may be refreshed as a practice and it can be with their witness statements. As I say, I need to look at it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, my recollection of that case is that in fact the Trial Chamber at first instance ruled that the Prosecution could not put a previous statement to a witness. The issue on the ground of appeal, as I remember it, was that that was a 92 bis witness and what was contended by the Defence was that portions that were not included in the 92 bis witness statement should not be put to the witness to refresh his memory; and that was the issue the Appeals Chamber decided on. I don't believe it set aside the thrust of the Trial Chamber's decision, that it was impermissible to put a statement to a witness to refresh his memory. I think the focus really was -- if I remember rightly, and I may be wrong - was focussed really on 92 bis and how that pans out in a 92 bis witness is called to give evidence in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. box. That of course can be checked by my learned friends who have the huge advantage of having access to a database which is far more reliable than our memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What the whole thing appears to be, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say before you go further, Mr. Nicholls and gentlemen, because we're starting to fall down to a fairly loose round of rebounding submissions, that this issue is one which has significance beyond this witness or may well have in this trial. It is a position which needs to be reviewed with a little care. The position in the countries of which I'm aware, and at a quick count that would be eight, is as I have indicated; I'm not familiar with the practice in your home jurisdiction. There is nothing of which I am aware in the Rules and nothing of which I am aware in any of the texts applicable to this jurisdiction. That being so, I think I should suggest that we would all benefit if counsel had a moment to reflect on this overnight and to come to the Chamber with some more detailed submissions. I think that would assist not only with this witness and to ensure that the issue concerning this witness is dealt with in accordance with law, but it would help in the future conduct of this trial. I have just been given a copy of the relevant part of the decision to which you referred and on first glance I don't know that it helps any position relevant to us. But reflection with greater care may throw more light upon that or any other decision that counsel are able to turn up. The question is: Can we usefully proceed with the witness on some other matters now or not, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would -- it would be my preference to adjourn and brief this issue rather than leave this point and try to come back to it. I think in -- that would be a more efficient use of time and a -- it may actually save some time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we can resolve this question, it certainly may save a lot of time because I've allowed you to go to the edge on this point several times so far despite the agitation from time to time of Mr. Khan. I have done it waiting for us to reach the crunch and this is it. I think we should grasp it and come to a decision. So the Chamber would indeed be grateful to counsel if they would give consideration to the matter, if feasible, to let us have some short written submissions, if they are desired, in the course of tomorrow morning, and if oral submissions thought useful after that, at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that it's necessary to adjourn overnight, but I think the point is worthy of it. We will adjourn now until 2.15. I'm sorry, this may have gone a little over your head, Mr. Karpuzi. We are having to adjourn now to sort out a question of law and we would ask that you return tomorrow to continue your evidence at 2.15. You'll be given more detailed guidance outside as to when to be back here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of February, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
